practice.title: Move Zeroes
practice.description:
A freezer inventory uses 0 for an empty slot. The loading screen needs occupied entries at the front without changing their order.

Given an integer array `nums`, move all `0`'s to the end of it while maintaining the relative order of the non-zero elements, and return the modified array.

examples.explanation: Non-zeros keep relative order [1, 3, 12] followed by zeros.

editorial.summary: Use a write pointer `pos` that places each non-zero element in order via in-place swap.
hints: Track the next index `pos` where a non-zero element belongs.
Whenever `nums[i] != 0`, swap `nums[pos]` and `nums[i]` and increment `pos`.
Everything from `pos` onward is automatically zero.
approachSteps: Iterate `i` from `0` to `len(nums) - 1`; if `nums[i] != 0`, swap `nums[pos]` with `nums[i]` and increment `pos`.
pitfalls: Avoid `list.remove(0)` inside a loop, which degrades to O(n^2).

practice.title: Spiral Matrix
practice.description:
A drone photographs a rectangular solar array from the outer edge toward the center. The controller needs the order in which to capture each cell.

Given an `m x n` `matrix`, return all elements of the matrix in clockwise spiral order.

examples.explanation: Clockwise outer ring followed by center 5.

editorial.summary: Maintain four shrinking boundaries `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`, peeling one edge at a time while checking boundaries before traversing bottom and left edges.
hints: Peel top row, right column, bottom row, left column in order.
Check `if top <= bottom` before traversing the bottom row.
Check `if left <= right` before traversing the left column.
approachSteps: Loop while `top <= bottom and left <= right` traversing 4 edges and shrinking each boundary.
pitfalls: For single-row or single-column remnants, skipping the boundary re-check duplicates elements.

practice.title: Rotate Image
practice.description:
A scanner mounted sideways sends a square pixel grid. The preview needs to show the result of a clockwise quarter turn.

You are given an `n x n` 2D `matrix` representing an image. Rotate the image by 90 degrees clockwise in-place and return the rotated matrix.

editorial.summary: Transpose the matrix across the main diagonal (`matrix[i][j] <-> matrix[j][i]`), then reverse every row.
hints: 90-degree clockwise rotation equals transpose followed by horizontal reflection.
During transpose, only iterate `j` from `i + 1` to `n - 1` so pairs are not swapped twice.
Reverse each row in-place.
approachSteps: Transpose upper triangle with lower triangle in-place.
pitfalls: Swapping for all `j` from `0` to `n-1` undoes the transpose.

practice.title: Set Matrix Zeroes
practice.description:
A quality check marks failing readings with 0. If a reading fails, the report suppresses all readings on its row and column.

Given an `m x n` integer `matrix`, if an element is `0`, set its entire row and column to `0` in-place using O(1) extra space, and return the modified matrix.

examples.explanation: Row 0, col 0, and col 3 become zero.

editorial.summary: Reuse row 0 and column 0 as in-place marker arrays, with two booleans tracking whether row 0 or column 0 originally contained any zeros.
hints: Store `first_row_zero` and `first_col_zero` before modifying the matrix.
Mark `matrix[r][0] = 0` and `matrix[0][c] = 0` for every interior zero.
Zero interior cells first, then zero row 0 and column 0 last.
approachSteps: Check if row 0 or col 0 initially contains a `0`.
Scan `(1..m-1, 1..n-1)` marking zeros in row 0 and col 0.
Zero interior cells whose row/col header is `0`.
Zero row 0 and/or col 0 according to the saved flags.
pitfalls: Zeroing row 0 or col 0 before interior cells destroys the markers.

practice.title: Insert Interval
practice.description:
A dispatcher tracks booked service windows in start order. A new request may touch or overlap more than one window.

You are given an array of non-overlapping `intervals` sorted by start time and a `new_interval`. Insert `new_interval` into `intervals` such that the result remains sorted and non-overlapping (merging overlapping intervals if necessary).
constraints: intervals is sorted in ascending order by start time.

editorial.summary: Perform a three-phase linear sweep: emit all intervals ending before `new_interval`, merge all overlapping intervals into `new_interval`, then append all remaining intervals.
hints: Intervals with `end < new_start` come strictly before.
Intervals with `start <= new_end` overlap and expand `[new_start, new_end]`.
All remaining intervals come strictly after.
approachSteps: Merge intervals with `intervals[i][0] <= ne` updating `ns = min(...)`, `ne = max(...)`.
Append `[ns, ne]` and extend with the remaining intervals.
pitfalls: Handle empty `intervals` cleanly.

referenceCode.code:
def insert_interval(intervals: list[list[int]], new_interval: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
    res = []
    i, n = 0, len(intervals)
    ns, ne = new_interval
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < ns:
        res.append(intervals[i])
        i += 1
    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= ne:
        ns = min(ns, intervals[i][0])
        ne = max(ne, intervals[i][1])
        i += 1
    res.append([ns, ne])
    res.extend(intervals[i:])
    return res

practice.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
practice.description:
A technician has only one test bench. Some bookings overlap, and the scheduler wants to cancel as few bookings as possible.

Given an array of `intervals`, return the minimum number of intervals you need to remove to make the rest of the intervals non-overlapping (touching endpoints like `[1, 2]` and `[2, 3]` are non-overlapping).

editorial.summary: Sort intervals by end time ascending and greedily keep every interval whose start is `>= prev_end`; the rest must be removed.
hints: Minimizing removals is equivalent to maximizing the number of non-overlapping intervals kept (Activity Selection).
Always keep the interval that finishes earliest to leave maximum room for future intervals.
Count overlaps where `start < prev_end`.
approachSteps: For `[s, e]` in `intervals[1:]`: if `s < prev_end`, increment `removed`; else set `prev_end = e`.
pitfalls: Sorting by start time instead of end time requires extra logic to keep the smaller end on overlap.

practice.title: Meeting Rooms II
practice.description:
An event coordinator has a set of requests. They need to know how many rooms to reserve so every session can go ahead.

Given an array of meeting time `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]`, return the minimum number of conference rooms required.

editorial.summary: Sort meetings by start time and track active meeting end times in a min-heap; reuse the earliest-ending room whenever `heap[0] <= start`.
hints: The number of rooms needed equals the maximum simultaneous overlapping meetings.
A min-heap of end times exposes the earliest room to become free in O(1).
Pop `heap[0]` if `heap[0] <= start`, then push `end`.
approachSteps: For `[s, e]` in `intervals`: if `ends` and `ends[0] <= s`, `heappop(ends)`; then `heappush(ends, e)`.
pitfalls: Meetings touching at `end == start` can reuse the same room (`<=`).

practice.title: Contiguous Array
practice.description:
A cable inspection records each measurement as either 0 or 1. The team wants its longest continuous stretch containing equal numbers of each result.

Given a binary array `nums` containing only `0`s and `1`s, return the maximum length of a contiguous subarray with an equal number of `0` and `1`.

editorial.summary: Treat `0` as `-1` and `1` as `+1`; whenever the running prefix balance repeats an earlier balance, the subarray in between has net sum `0` (equal 0s and 1s).
hints: Store the FIRST index where each running balance appeared.
Seed `first_seen = {0: -1}` before index 0.
approachSteps: For `i, x` in `enumerate(nums)`, update `bal += 1 if x == 1 else -1`.
If `bal in first_seen`, update `best = max(best, i - first_seen[bal])`; else record `first_seen[bal] = i`.
pitfalls: Never overwrite `first_seen[bal]` because keeping the earliest index maximizes subarray length.

practice.title: 4Sum
practice.description: Given an array `nums` of `n` integers and an integer `target`, return all unique quadruplets `[nums[a], nums[b], nums[c], nums[d]]` with distinct indices that sum to `target`.

editorial.summary: Sort the array, fix two outer indices skipping duplicates, and use two pointers on the remaining suffix.
hints: Sort `nums` first.
Skip duplicate values for `i`, `j`, `l`, and `r`.
Use 64-bit integers in Java/C++ since four 10^9 numbers can overflow 32-bit int.
approachSteps: Fix `i` in `0..n-4` and `j` in `i+1..n-3` skipping duplicates.
Run two pointers `l = j + 1`, `r = n - 1` looking for `target - nums[i] - nums[j]`.
pitfalls: Return `[]` immediately when `len(nums) < 4`.

practice.title: Next Permutation
practice.description:
A test lab assigns a run to each ordering of job IDs. The scheduler needs to advance to the next ordering in its usual sorted order.

Given an array of integers `nums`, rearrange it in-place into its lexicographically next greater permutation (or the lowest sorted order if no greater permutation exists), and return `nums`.

examples.explanation: Already highest, so wraps to lowest permutation.

editorial.summary: Find the rightmost ascent `nums[i] < nums[i + 1]`, swap `nums[i]` with the rightmost element `> nums[i]`, and reverse the suffix `nums[i + 1:]`.
hints: Scan right-to-left to find the first dip `i` where `nums[i] < nums[i + 1]`.
If `i >= 0`, scan right-to-left for the first `j` with `nums[j] > nums[i]` and swap them.
Reverse `nums[i + 1:]` so the suffix is in smallest ascending order.
approachSteps: If `i >= 0`, find rightmost `j` with `nums[j] > nums[i]` and swap `nums[i], nums[j]`.
pitfalls: Use `<=` (not `<`) when skipping duplicates during the backward scans.

practice.title: Pascal's Triangle
practice.description: Given an integer `num_rows`, return the first `num_rows` of Pascal's triangle.

examples.explanation: Each interior number is the sum of the two numbers directly above it.

editorial.summary: Build each row from the previous row with `1` at both ends and `prev[j - 1] + prev[j]` in the interior.
hints: Row `r` has length `r + 1` with `1` at indices `0` and `r`.
Every interior element `j` equals `prev[j - 1] + prev[j]`.
Build row-by-row from `0` to `num_rows - 1`.
approachSteps: For each subsequent row, construct `[1] + [prev[j-1] + prev[j] for j in range(1, len(prev))] + [1]`.
pitfalls: Handle `num_rows == 1` cleanly.

referenceCode.code:
def generate_pascal(num_rows: int) -> list[list[int]]:
    tri = [[1]]
    for _ in range(1, num_rows):
        prev = tri[-1]
        row = [1] + [prev[j - 1] + prev[j] for j in range(1, len(prev))] + [1]
        tri.append(row)
    return tri

practice.title: Merge Sorted Array
practice.description:
A device stores a sorted event batch with spare capacity at the end. A second sorted batch arrives and must be integrated into the first buffer.

You are given two sorted integer arrays `nums1` (length `m + n`, with trailing `0` placeholders) and `nums2` (length `n`), along with `m` and `n`. Merge `nums2` into `nums1` in-place in non-decreasing order and return `nums1`.

examples.explanation: Merged from back to front without extra space.

editorial.summary: Fill `nums1` from the back (`m + n - 1` down to `0`) by comparing the largest remaining elements of `nums1` and `nums2`.
hints: Filling forward overwrites unread values in `nums1`.
Filling backward writes into the empty trailing zeros first.
Once `j < 0` (`nums2` exhausted), the remaining elements of `nums1` are already in place.
approachSteps: While `j >= 0`, write the larger of `nums1[i]` (if `i >= 0`) and `nums2[j]` to `nums1[k]` and decrement pointers.
pitfalls: Always check `i >= 0` before reading `nums1[i]`.

practice.title: Intersection of Two Arrays II
practice.description:
Two stores report item IDs including repeated items. A reconciler needs the quantities that occur in both reports.

Given two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2`, return an array of their intersection where each element appears as many times as it shows in both arrays. You may return the result in any order.

examples.explanation: 4 and 9 appear at least once in both.

editorial.summary: Count frequencies in the smaller array using a hash map, then scan the larger array decrementing counts on each match.
hints: Count the smaller array to minimize memory usage.
For each `x` in the second array, if `counts[x] > 0`, append `x` and decrement `counts[x]`.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Decrement the count after each match so duplicates aren't over-emitted. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n + m) time and O(min(n, m)) space limits.
approachSteps: Iterate `x` in `nums2`: if `counts[x] > 0`, append `x` to `res` and decrement `counts[x]`.
pitfalls: Decrement the count after each match so duplicates aren't over-emitted.

practice.title: Word Pattern
practice.description:
A deployment tool assigns an alias letter to each service name. A trace is valid only if each letter maps to one service and each service has one letter.

Given a `pattern` and a space-separated string `s`, return `true` if `s` follows the exact same bijection between each letter in `pattern` and each non-empty word in `s`.

examples.explanation: a and b cannot both map to "dog".

editorial.summary: Split `s` into words, verify equal length with `pattern`, and enforce a bidirectional mapping between characters and words.
hints: First check `len(words) == len(pattern)`.
Use two dictionaries `c2w` and `w2c` to verify a bijection.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Don't forget to check that the number of words equals `len(pattern)`. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n) time and O(n) space limits.
approachSteps: Check and populate `c2w` and `w2c` for every `(ch, w)` pair.
pitfalls: Don't forget to check that the number of words equals `len(pattern)`.

practice.title: Ransom Note
practice.description:
A sign maker wants to assemble a short message using a supply of printed letters. Each letter can be used once.

Given two strings `ransom_note` and `magazine`, return `true` if `ransom_note` can be constructed by using the letters from `magazine` (each letter in `magazine` can only be used once), and `false` otherwise.
constraints: Both consist of lowercase English letters.

editorial.summary: Count character frequencies in `magazine` and verify every character in `ransom_note` has sufficient count.
hints: If `len(ransom_note) > len(magazine)`, return `False` immediately.
Count `magazine` letters and decrement as you scan `ransom_note`.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Check `< 0` after decrementing to catch missing letters. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n + m) time and O(1) space limits.
approachSteps: For each `ch` in `ransom_note`, decrement `counts[ch]`; if `< 0`, return `False`.
pitfalls: Check `< 0` after decrementing to catch missing letters.

practice.title: Find All Anagrams in a String
practice.description:
A text index checks where a signal could occur with its letters shuffled. It needs the starting position of every matching window.

Given two strings `s` and `p`, return an array of all the start indices of `p`'s anagrams in `s` in ascending order.

examples.explanation: "cba" at 0 and "bac" at 6 are anagrams of "abc".

constraints: s and p consist of lowercase English letters.

editorial.summary: Slide a fixed-length window of size `len(p)` across `s`, maintaining a 26-element frequency array and comparing against `p`'s frequency array in O(26) = O(1) per step.
hints: If `len(p) > len(s)`, return `[]`.
Maintain two 26-element arrays `p_cnt` and `win_cnt`.
Each step adds `s[i]` and removes `s[i - len(p)]`.
approachSteps: Build `p_cnt` and initial `win_cnt` for the first `len(p)` chars.
Slide `i` from `len(p)` to `len(s) - 1`, updating counts and recording `i - len(p) + 1` on match.
pitfalls: Return `[]` early when `len(p) > len(s)`.

practice.title: Fruit Into Baskets
practice.description:
A picker starts at any tree in a row and visits consecutive trees. Its two baskets can each accept exactly one fruit type.

Given an integer array `fruits` where `fruits[i]` is the type of fruit the `i`-th tree produces, return the length of the longest contiguous subarray containing at most `2` distinct fruit types.

examples.explanation: All 3 trees have at most 2 fruit types.

editorial.summary: Find the longest subarray with at most 2 distinct values using a sliding window and a frequency map.
hints: Track counts of each fruit type inside `[l.r]`.
When `len(counts) > 2`, decrement `counts[fruits[l]]`, delete the key if it hits `0`, and increment `l`.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Delete keys whose count drops to `0` so `len(counts)` accurately reflects distinct types. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n) time and O(1) space limits.
pitfalls: Delete keys whose count drops to `0` so `len(counts)` accurately reflects distinct types.

referenceCode.code:
from collections import defaultdict

def total_fruit(fruits: list[int]) -> int:
    counts = defaultdict(int)
    l = best = 0
    for r, f in enumerate(fruits):
        counts[f] += 1
        while len(counts) > 2:
            left_f = fruits[l]
            counts[left_f] -= 1
            if counts[left_f] == 0:
                del counts[left_f]
            l += 1
        best = max(best, r - l + 1)
    return best

practice.title: Boats to Save People
practice.description:
A ferry shuttle must carry everyone across a river. A shuttle can carry at most two riders and has a strict weight rating.

You are given an array `people` where `people[i]` is the weight of the `i`-th person, and each boat carries at most two people with combined weight at most `limit`. Return the minimum number of boats to carry every given person.

editorial.summary: Sort weights and greedily pair the heaviest remaining person with the lightest remaining person whenever their sum is `<= limit`.
hints: Each boat holds at most 2 people.
If the lightest person cannot pair with the heaviest, nobody else can pair with the heaviest either.
Always board the heaviest person `r`, and also board `l` if `people[l] + people[r] <= limit`.
approachSteps: While `l <= r`: if `people[l] + people[r] <= limit`, `l += 1`; always `r -= 1` and `boats += 1`.
pitfalls: Use `l <= r` so a single remaining middle person gets a boat.

practice.title: Backspace String Compare
practice.description:
An editor recorded two streams of keystrokes. Its comparison view needs to know whether the streams left identical text on screen.

Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `true` if they are equal when both are typed into empty text editors where `'#'` means a backspace character.
constraints: s and t contain only lowercase letters and '#' characters.

editorial.summary: Scan both strings backward skipping characters canceled by `'#'` to compare in O(1) space (or build final stacks).
hints: Iterating in reverse tells you immediately how many upcoming characters must be skipped.
Maintain a `skip` counter for each string.
Compare the next surviving characters from right to left.
approachSteps: Define generator yielding surviving characters from right to left.
Compare pairs from both generators using `zip_longest`.
pitfalls: Backspacing on an empty editor simply leaves it empty.

practice.title: Roman to Integer
practice.description: Given a valid Roman numeral string `s` (in range 1 to 3999), convert it to an integer.
constraints: s is a valid Roman numeral in [1, 3999].

editorial.summary: Scan left-to-right: if the current symbol has a smaller value than the next symbol, subtract it; otherwise add it.
hints: Subtractive pairs like `IV`, `IX`, `XL`, `CM` always have `val[i] < val[i + 1]`.
All other symbols simply add to the total.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Guard `i + 1 < len(s)` before inspecting the next character. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n) time and O(1) space limits.
approachSteps: For each index `i`, subtract `val[s[i]]` if `i + 1 < n and val[s[i]] < val[s[i + 1]]`, else add it.
pitfalls: Guard `i + 1 < len(s)` before inspecting the next character.

practice.title: Integer to Roman
practice.description: Given an integer `num` in the range `[1, 3999]`, convert it to a Roman numeral.

editorial.summary: Include the 6 subtractive tokens (`CM`, `CD`, `XC`, `XL`, `IX`, `IV`) in a descending lookup table and greedily emit the largest value fitting into `num`.
hints: There are 13 canonical Roman tokens from 1000 down to 1.
Use `count, num = divmod(num, val)` for each token.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Include all 6 subtractive pairs in strictly descending order. Verify your solution strictly meets O(1) time and O(1) space limits.
approachSteps: Define descending `(value, symbol)` table of 13 entries.
For each `(v, sym)`, append `sym * (num // v)` and update `num %= v`.
pitfalls: Include all 6 subtractive pairs in strictly descending order.

practice.title: Multiply Strings
practice.description:
A calculator receives decimal amounts too long for its built-in integer types. It must report their product as decimal text.

Given two non-negative integers `num1` and `num2` represented as strings, return the product of `num1` and `num2`, also represented as a string, without converting the inputs directly to big integers.
constraints: Digits only, no leading zeros except "0".

editorial.summary: Allocate a digit array of length `m + n`; the product of digits at `i` and `j` contributes directly to positions `i + j + 1` (ones) and `i + j` (carry).
hints: The product of an `m`-digit and `n`-digit number has at most `m + n` digits.
Iterate `i` and `j` backward so carries propagate cleanly.
Strip leading zeros, returning `"0"` if either input is `"0"`.
approachSteps: For `i` from `m-1` down to `0` and `j` from `n-1` down to `0`, add `d1 * d2 + pos[i + j + 1]` and split into `pos[i + j + 1]` and `pos[i + j]`.
pitfalls: Strip leading zeros carefully without emptying `"0"`.

practice.title: Add Binary
practice.description:
Two counters export positive quantities as binary text. A collector needs their combined value in the same format.

Given two binary strings `a` and `b`, return their sum as a binary string.
constraints: a and b consist only of '0' or '1'.

editorial.summary: Walk both strings from right to left summing bit values plus `carry`, emitting `total % 2`, and reversing the collected bits.
hints: Process from least-significant bit (end of string) backward.
Continue while `i >= 0 or j >= 0 or carry`.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Do not forget the final carry bit when both strings end. Verify your solution strictly meets O(max(n, m)) time and O(max(n, m)) space limits.
approachSteps: Loop summing available bits and `carry`, append `str(s & 1)`, set `carry = s >> 1`.
pitfalls: Do not forget the final carry bit when both strings end.

practice.title: String Compression
practice.description:
An encoder needs to compact runs of identical characters in a fixed buffer. Decodeability depends on recording both the character and its run length.

Given an array of characters `chars`, compress consecutive repeating characters in-place: a single character stays as is, while a group of length `> 1` is followed by the digits of its count. Return the compressed list of characters.

examples.explanation: Single character has no count digit.

constraints: chars[i] is a printable ASCII character.

editorial.summary: Use read and write pointers to measure each run of identical characters, writing the character and each digit of `str(count)` when `count > 1`.
hints: Counts >= 10 must be split into individual character digits (`'1'`, `'2'`).
Write pointer never overtakes read pointer.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Split multi-digit counts into separate single-character elements. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n) time and O(1) space limits.
approachSteps: Write `chars[read]` and digits of `end - read` if `> 1`; advance `read = end`.
pitfalls: Split multi-digit counts into separate single-character elements.

referenceCode.code:
def compress_chars(chars: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    write = read = 0
    n = len(chars)
    while read < n:
        ch = chars[read]
        end = read
        while end < n and chars[end] == ch:
            end += 1
        chars[write] = ch
        write += 1
        cnt = end - read
        if cnt > 1:
            for d in str(cnt):
                chars[write] = d
                write += 1
        read = end
    return chars[:write]

practice.title: Remove K Digits
practice.description:
A migration removes exactly k digits from a record number while keeping the order of the remaining digits. The destination system needs the smallest possible result.

Given a string `num` representing a non-negative integer and an integer `k`, return the smallest possible integer as a string after removing `k` digits from `num` (with no leading zeros).

editorial.summary: Maintain a monotonic increasing digit stack: pop larger previous digits while `k > 0`, trim any remaining `k` digits from the end, and strip leading zeros.
hints: Removing a larger digit to the left of a smaller digit always reduces the number.
If digits are already non-decreasing, remove the remaining `k` digits from the right.
Return `"0"` if stripping leading zeros leaves an empty string.
approachSteps: For each digit `d` in `num`: while `k > 0 and stack and stack[-1] > d`, pop and decrement `k`; push `d`.
pitfalls: Handle leftover `k > 0` (e.g. `num = '112', k = 1`) and all-zero outcomes.

practice.title: Sum of Subarray Minimums
practice.description: Given an array of integers `arr`, find the sum of `min(b)` over every contiguous subarray `b` of `arr`. Return the answer modulo `10^9 + 7`.

examples.explanation: Sum of all subarray minimums is 444.

editorial.summary: Use a monotonic increasing stack to compute each element's contribution `arr[mid] * (mid - left) * (right - mid)` using strict `<` on one side and `<=` on the other to avoid double-counting duplicates.
hints: Each element `arr[mid]` is the minimum of `(mid - prev_smaller) * (next_smaller_or_eq - mid)` subarrays.
Append a sentinel `0` at the end to flush all elements.
Take modulo `10^9 + 7`.
approachSteps: While `stack and arr[stack[-1]] >= x`, pop `mid`, set `left = stack[-1] if stack else -1`, and add `arr[mid] * (mid - left) * (i - mid)`.
pitfalls: Use `>=` when popping so duplicate values are uniquely owned by one boundary.

referenceCode.code:
def sum_subarray_mins(arr: list[int]) -> int:
    MOD = 10**9 + 7
    stack = []
    ans = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(arr + [0]):
        while stack and arr[stack[-1]] >= x:
            mid = stack.pop()
            left = stack[-1] if stack else -1
            ans = (ans + arr[mid] * (mid - left) * (i - mid)) % MOD
        stack.append(i)
    return ans

practice.title: Maximal Rectangle
practice.description: Given a `rows x cols` binary `matrix` filled with `'0'`s and `'1'`s, find the largest rectangle containing only `'1'`s and return its area.

editorial.summary: Build a running column-height histogram row by row and apply the O(cols) monotonic stack Largest Rectangle in Histogram algorithm to each row.
hints: For each row, `heights[c] = heights[c] + 1` if `matrix[r][c] == '1'` else `0`.
Run Largest Rectangle in Histogram on `heights` after each row.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Reset `heights[c] = 0` whenever a `'0'` cell is encountered. Verify your solution strictly meets O(rows * cols) time and O(cols) space limits.
approachSteps: Run monotonic increasing stack over `heights` updating `best`.
pitfalls: Reset `heights[c] = 0` whenever a `'0'` cell is encountered.

practice.title: Basic Calculator
practice.description: Given a string `s` representing a valid expression with integers, `'+'`, `'-'`, `'('`, `')'`, and spaces, evaluate it and return the result.

editorial.summary: Maintain running `res`, `num`, and `sign`, pushing `(res, sign)` onto a stack on `'('` and combining on `')'`.
hints: Unary minus works naturally because `res` starts at `0` before `'-'`.
On `'('`, save `(res, sign)` and reset `res = 0, sign = 1`.
On `')'`, flush `num`, multiply by popped `sign`, and add popped `res`.
pitfalls: Flush the last `num` after the loop ends.

referenceCode.code:
def calculate_expr(s: str) -> int:
    stack = []
    res = num = 0
    sign = 1
    for ch in s:
        if ch.isdigit():
            num = num * 10 + int(ch)
        elif ch == '+':
            res += sign * num
            num = 0
            sign = 1
        elif ch == '-':
            res += sign * num
            num = 0
            sign = -1
        elif ch == '(':
            stack.append((res, sign))
            res = 0
            sign = 1
        elif ch == ')':
            res += sign * num
            num = 0
            prev_res, prev_sign = stack.pop()
            res = prev_res + prev_sign * res
    return res + sign * num

practice.title: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String
practice.description: Given a string `s`, repeatedly remove pairs of adjacent equal letters until no more can be removed, and return the final string.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.

editorial.summary: Use a character stack: if the top matches the incoming character, pop it; otherwise push.
hints: A stack automatically exposes newly adjacent characters after a cancellation.
Join the stack at the end.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Only remove pairs (2 identical characters), not all 3 of `'aaa'` (which becomes `'a'`). Verify your solution strictly meets O(n) time and O(n) space limits.
approachSteps: For each `ch` in `s`: if `stack and stack[-1] == ch`, pop; else append `ch`.
pitfalls: Only remove pairs (2 identical characters), not all 3 of `'aaa'` (which becomes `'a'`).

practice.title: Minimum Remove to Make Valid Parentheses
practice.description: Given a string `s` of `'('`, `')'`, and lowercase English characters, remove the minimum number of unmatched parentheses (removing unmatched `')'` immediately and rightmost unmatched `'('` at the end) so that the resulting string is valid.

examples.explanation: The trailing ')' is unmatched and removed.

constraints: s[i] is '(', ')', or a lowercase letter.

editorial.summary: Track indices of unmatched `'('` on a stack and record indices of unmatched `')'` in a removal set, then rebuild the string omitting all marked indices.
hints: Store index `i` on the stack for every `'('`.
If `')'` sees an empty stack, add `i` to `remove`; otherwise pop a matching `'('`.
Any indices left in the stack at the end are unmatched `'('` and also go into `remove`.
approachSteps: Scan `s` pushing `'('` indices, popping on matched `')'`, or marking unmatched `')'`.
Union remaining `stack` into `remove` and join surviving characters.
pitfalls: Convert `remove` to a set so membership checks during reconstruction are O(1).

practice.title: Score of Parentheses
practice.description: Given a balanced parentheses string `s`, return its score where `"()"` has score `1`, `AB` has score `A + B`, and `(A)` has score `2 * A`.
constraints: s is a balanced parentheses string.

editorial.summary: Every core pair `"()"` at nesting depth `d` contributes `2^d` to the total score; sum `1 << depth` whenever `s[i - 1:i + 1] == '()'`.
hints: Distributing `2 * (A + B)` gives `2A + 2B`, so only innermost `()` cores contribute weight.
Track nesting `depth`: increment on `'('`, decrement on `')'`.
When `s[i] == ')'` and `s[i - 1] == '('`, add `1 << depth`.
approachSteps: Iterate `i, ch` over `enumerate(s)`: increment `depth` on `'('`; on `')'`, decrement `depth` and if `s[i - 1] == '('`, add `1 << depth`.
pitfalls: Decrement `depth` BEFORE computing `1 << depth` so top-level `"()"` adds `1 << 0 = 1`.

practice.title: Palindrome Linked List
practice.description:
An inspection trail is represented as a chain of readings. An auditor wants to know whether it reads the same from both ends.

Given the values of a singly linked list `values`, return `true` if the linked list is a palindrome, or `false` otherwise.

examples.explanation: Reads the same forward and backward.

editorial.summary: Find the midpoint with fast/slow pointers, reverse the second half in-place, and compare both halves node by node.
hints: Slow/fast pointers locate the middle in O(n) time.
Reverse the second half to compare in O(1) space.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Odd-length lists have a middle node that does not need to match anything. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n) time and O(1) space limits.
approachSteps: Compare elements symmetrically from both ends (or reverse second half of linked list).
Return `True` iff all mirrored pairs match.
pitfalls: Odd-length lists have a middle node that does not need to match anything.

referenceCode.code:
def is_palindrome_list(values: list[int]) -> bool:
    return values == values[::-1]

practice.title: Search Insert Position
practice.description:
A warehouse keeps numeric bin IDs in sorted order. A new scan needs either an existing bin’s index or the position to insert a new bin.

Given a sorted array of distinct integers `nums` and a `target` value, return the index if `target` is found. If not, return the index where it would be if it were inserted in order, in `O(log n)` time.
constraints: nums contains distinct values sorted ascending.

editorial.summary: Find the first index `l` where `nums[l] >= target` (lower bound) using binary search on `[0, len(nums)]`.
hints: Set `r = len(nums)` so targets greater than all elements can return `len(nums)`.
Shrink `[l, r)` until `l == r`.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Upper bound must include `len(nums)` for insertion after the last element. Verify your solution strictly meets O(log n) time and O(1) space limits.
approachSteps: While `l < r`, compute `mid = (l + r) // 2`; if `nums[mid] < target`, `l = mid + 1`; else `r = mid`.
pitfalls: Upper bound must include `len(nums)` for insertion after the last element.

practice.title: Sqrt(x)
practice.description: Given a non-negative integer `x`, return the square root of `x` rounded down to the nearest integer without using any built-in exponent or square root operator.

editorial.summary: Binary search for the largest integer `mid` in `[0, x]` satisfying `mid * mid <= x`.
hints: If `x < 2`, return `x` directly.
Binary search in `[1, x // 2]` comparing `mid * mid` with `x`.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: In 32-bit languages, compare `mid <= x / mid` instead of `mid * mid <= x` to avoid overflow. Verify your solution strictly meets O(log x) time and O(1) space limits.
approachSteps: While `l <= r`, compute `mid`; if `mid * mid <= x`, `l = mid + 1`; else `r = mid - 1`.
pitfalls: In 32-bit languages, compare `mid <= x / mid` instead of `mid * mid <= x` to avoid overflow.

practice.title: Find Peak Element
practice.description: A peak element is strictly greater than its neighbors (assuming out-of-bounds neighbors are `-inf`). Given an array `nums` where `nums[i] != nums[i + 1]`, find a peak element's index in `O(log n)` time.

examples.explanation: nums[2] = 3 is strictly greater than 2 and 1.

constraints: nums[i] != nums[i + 1] for all valid i.

editorial.summary: Compare `nums[mid]` with `nums[mid + 1]`: always climb uphill (`l = mid + 1` if rising, `r = mid` if falling) until `l == r`.
hints: If `nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]`, a peak is guaranteed to exist on the right side.
Otherwise a peak is guaranteed on the left side including `mid`.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Because `l < r`, `mid + 1` is always strictly in bounds. Verify your solution strictly meets O(log n) time and O(1) space limits.
approachSteps: While `l < r`, compute `mid = (l + r) // 2`; if `nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]`, `l = mid + 1`; else `r = mid`.
pitfalls: Because `l < r`, `mid + 1` is always strictly in bounds.

practice.title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
practice.description:
An operations planner has a fixed order of parcels and a delivery deadline. The goal is to rent the lightest truck that can finish in time.

Packages with weights `weights[i]` must be shipped in order on a conveyor belt within `days` days. Return the least weight capacity of the ship that will result in all packages being shipped within `days` days.

editorial.summary: Binary search the ship capacity in `[max(weights), sum(weights)]`, greedily packing each day up to `mid` to count required days.
hints: Capacity must be at least `max(weights)` so the heaviest single package fits.
Greedy linear packing checks feasibility in O(n).
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Initialize `needed = 1` (the first day) before scanning `weights`. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n log(sum(weights))) time and O(1) space limits.
approachSteps: For candidate `mid`, count days needed by greedily accumulating weights up to `mid`.
pitfalls: Initialize `needed = 1` (the first day) before scanning `weights`.

practice.title: Split Array Largest Sum
practice.description: Given an integer array `nums` of non-negative integers and an integer `k`, split `nums` into `k` non-empty contiguous subarrays such that the largest sum among these `k` subarrays is minimized. Return the minimized largest sum.

editorial.summary: Binary search the maximum allowed subarray sum `mid` in `[max(nums), sum(nums)]` and verify greedily whether `nums` can be partitioned into `<= k` subarrays.
hints: Feasibility is monotonic in `mid`.
Greedily start a new subarray whenever `cur + x > mid`.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Lower bound must be `max(nums)` so every single element fits in a subarray. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n log(sum(nums))) time and O(1) space limits.
approachSteps: Count greedy partitions for `mid`; if `parts <= k`, `r = mid`; else `l = mid + 1`.
pitfalls: Lower bound must be `max(nums)` so every single element fits in a subarray.

practice.title: Single Element in a Sorted Array
practice.description: You are given a sorted array `nums` consisting of only integers where every element appears exactly twice, except for one element which appears exactly once. Return the single element in `O(log n)` time and `O(1)` space.

examples.explanation: 2 appears once while all others appear twice.

editorial.summary: Before the single element, pairs start at even indices `(2k, 2k+1)`; after it, pairs start at odd indices. Snap `mid` to even (`mid & ~1`) and check `nums[mid] == nums[mid + 1]`.
hints: Force `mid` to be even (`if mid % 2 == 1: mid -= 1`).
If `nums[mid] == nums[mid + 1]`, the single element is to the right (`l = mid + 2`); else `r = mid`.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Ensure `mid` is even before comparing `mid` with `mid + 1`. Verify your solution strictly meets O(log n) time and O(1) space limits.
approachSteps: While `l < r`, compute even `mid = (l + r) // 2` (`mid -= mid % 2`).
pitfalls: Ensure `mid` is even before comparing `mid` with `mid + 1`.

practice.title: Search a 2D Matrix II
practice.description: Write an efficient algorithm that searches for `target` in an `m x n` integer `matrix` where every row is sorted left-to-right and every column is sorted top-to-bottom.
constraints: Rows and columns are sorted ascending.

editorial.summary: Start at the top-right corner `(0, n - 1)`: move left if `val > target`, move down if `val < target`, eliminating one row or column per step.
hints: At the top-right corner, moving left strictly decreases and moving down strictly increases.
Total steps are at most `m + n`.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Starting at top-left or bottom-right does not give a unique direction to prune. Verify your solution strictly meets O(m + n) time and O(1) space limits.
approachSteps: While `r < m and c >= 0`: return `True` if equal, `c -= 1` if `val > target`, else `r += 1`.
pitfalls: Starting at top-left or bottom-right does not give a unique direction to prune.

practice.title: H-Index II
practice.description: Given an array of integers `citations` sorted in ascending order where `citations[i]` is the number of citations a researcher received for their `i`-th paper, return the researcher's h-index in `O(log n)` time.

examples.explanation: 3 papers have at least 3 citations each.

editorial.summary: Find the smallest index `i` such that `citations[i] >= n - i`; then the h-index is `n - i`.
hints: At index `i`, there are `n - i` papers with at least `citations[i]` citations.
Binary search for the first index where `citations[mid] >= n - mid`.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Handle all-zero citations returning `0` cleanly (`l == n`). Verify your solution strictly meets O(log n) time and O(1) space limits.
approachSteps: While `l < r`, compute `mid = (l + r) // 2`; if `citations[mid] >= n - mid`, `r = mid`; else `l = mid + 1`.
pitfalls: Handle all-zero citations returning `0` cleanly (`l == n`).

practice.title: Largest Number
practice.description: Given a list of non-negative integers `nums`, arrange them such that they form the largest number and return it as a string.

editorial.summary: Convert numbers to strings and sort with custom comparator placing `a` before `b` iff `a + b > b + a`.
hints: Comparing `a + b` vs `b + a` defines a strict weak ordering.
If the largest element is `'0'`, return `'0'` instead of `'000'`.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Handle `[0, 0]` returning `'0'`, not `'00'`. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n log n * k) time and O(n * k) space limits.
approachSteps: Sort using `cmp_to_key` comparing `b + a` vs `a + b`.
pitfalls: Handle `[0, 0]` returning `'0'`, not `'00'`.

practice.title: Same Tree
practice.description: Given two binary trees in trimmed level-order representation `p` and `q`, return `true` if they are structurally identical and have the same node values.

editorial.summary: Recursively check that both nodes are `None`, or both exist with equal values and identical left and right subtrees.
hints: Two `None` nodes match; one `None` and one non-`None` do not.
Compare `a.val == b.val` and recurse on left and right.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Handle empty trees returning `True`. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n) time and O(h) space limits.
approachSteps: Recursively compare `(n1, n2)` for structural and value equality.
pitfalls: Handle empty trees returning `True`.

practice.title: Path Sum
practice.description: Given a binary tree in level-order representation `tree` and an integer `target_sum`, return `true` if the tree has a root-to-leaf path such that adding up all values along the path equals `target_sum`.

examples.input: tree = [5, 4, 8, 11, null, 13, 4, 7, 2, null, null, null, 1], target_sum = 22

testCases.input: tree = [5, 4, 8, 11, null, 13, 4, 7, 2, null, null, null, 1], target_sum = 22

editorial.summary: Subtract `node.val` from `remaining` down the tree and return `True` only at a true leaf (`not node.left and not node.right`) where `remaining == node.val`.
hints: An empty tree has no root-to-leaf path, even if `target_sum == 0`.
A node with one child is NOT a leaf.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Do not treat a node with a single missing child as a leaf. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n) time and O(h) space limits.
approachSteps: In `dfs(node, rem)`: if `not node`, return `False`; if leaf, return `rem == node.val`; else recurse on left or right with `rem - node.val`.
pitfalls: Do not treat a node with a single missing child as a leaf.

practice.title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
practice.description: Given a binary tree in level-order representation `tree`, a node `X` is named good if on the path from root to `X` there are no nodes with a value strictly greater than `X`. Return the number of good nodes.

editorial.summary: Pass `max_so_far` down a top-down DFS; count `1` whenever `node.val >= max_so_far` and propagate `max(max_so_far, node.val)`.
hints: The root is always good.
Initialize `max_so_far = root.val` to handle negative node values.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Never initialize `mx = 0` because node values can be negative. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n) time and O(h) space limits.
approachSteps: Recurse `dfs(node, mx)`: add `1` if `node.val >= mx`, update `nmx = max(mx, node.val)`, sum left and right.
pitfalls: Never initialize `mx = 0` because node values can be negative.

practice.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
practice.description: Given a binary tree of unique values in level-order representation `tree` and two node values `p` and `q`, return the value of their Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA).
constraints: p and q exist in the tree.

editorial.summary: In post-order DFS, return `node` immediately if it equals `p` or `q`; if both left and right subtrees return non-null, `node` is the LCA.
hints: Unlike a BST, you cannot prune by value comparisons.
If only one side returns a node, bubble that node upward.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Return `node.val` (int), not the `TreeNode` object. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n) time and O(h) space limits.
approachSteps: In `dfs(node)`: return `node` if `not node` or `node.val in (p, q)`.
Compute `l = dfs(left)`, `r = dfs(right)`; return `node` if `l and r`, else `l or r`.
pitfalls: Return `node.val` (int), not the `TreeNode` object.

practice.title: Flood Fill
practice.description:
A map editor wants to recolor the connected region under the cursor without affecting disconnected patches of the same original color.

Given an `m x n` integer grid `image`, a starting pixel `(sr, sc)`, and a new `color`, perform a 4-directional flood fill starting from `(sr, sc)` replacing all connected pixels of the original color with `color`, and return the modified image.

editorial.summary: If `image[sr][sc] == color`, return immediately to prevent an infinite loop; otherwise BFS 4-directional neighbors matching `orig`.
hints: Check `if orig == color: return image` first!.
Recolor cells as they are enqueued.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Omitting `if orig == color: return` causes infinite looping. Verify your solution strictly meets O(m * n) time and O(m * n) space limits.
approachSteps: Set `image[sr][sc] = color` and BFS all 4-directional neighbors equal to `orig`.
pitfalls: Omitting `if orig == color: return` causes infinite looping.

practice.title: Max Area of Island
practice.description: Given an `m x n` binary matrix `grid` where `1` represents land and `0` represents water, return the maximum area (number of 4-directionally connected `1`s) of an island in `grid`, or `0` if there is no island.

editorial.summary: Flood-fill each unvisited land component, counting cells visited per component and tracking the maximum area.
hints: Mark visited cells `0` to avoid revisiting.
Sum the component size during BFS/DFS and update `best`.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Diagonal cells are NOT connected. Verify your solution strictly meets O(m * n) time and O(m * n) space limits.
approachSteps: Loop over all `(r, c)`; on `1`, run BFS counting cells and marking them `0`.
pitfalls: Diagonal cells are NOT connected.

practice.title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
practice.description: Given an `m x n` matrix `heights` where the Pacific Ocean touches the top and left edges and the Atlantic Ocean touches the bottom and right edges, water can flow to 4-directional neighbors of equal or lower height. Return all `[r, c]` coordinates from which water can flow to both oceans.

examples.explanation: Cells forming the ridge can drain to both oceans.

editorial.summary: Run two reverse-uphill BFS traversals starting from the Pacific border and the Atlantic border (moving to neighbors with `height >= curr`), then intersect the two reachable sets.
hints: Flowing downhill from a cell to an ocean is equivalent to climbing uphill from the ocean to that cell.
Intersect `pac_visited & atl_visited`.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Reverse traversal requires `heights[nr][nc] >= heights[r][c]`. Verify your solution strictly meets O(m * n) time and O(m * n) space limits.
approachSteps: BFS uphill from Pacific edges `(r=0 or c=0)`.
BFS uphill from Atlantic edges `(r=m-1 or c=n-1)`.
Return sorted `[r, c]` in both sets.
pitfalls: Reverse traversal requires `heights[nr][nc] >= heights[r][c]`.

practice.title: Keys and Rooms
practice.description:
A building simulation begins with one unlocked room. Opening a room may reveal keys to others, and the operator needs to know if every room is reachable.

There are `n` rooms labeled `0` to `n - 1`; only room `0` is unlocked initially. `rooms[i]` lists the keys found inside room `i`. Return `true` if you can visit all `n` rooms.

editorial.summary: Perform BFS/DFS starting from room `0` and check whether `len(visited) == len(rooms)`.
hints: Rooms are nodes and keys are directed edges.
Check full reachability from node `0`.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: A room may contain a key to itself; `visited` prevents infinite loops. Verify your solution strictly meets O(V + E) time and O(V) space limits.
approachSteps: Pop room `u`, add unvisited keys `v` in `rooms[u]` to `visited` and `stack`.
pitfalls: A room may contain a key to itself; `visited` prevents infinite loops.

practice.title: Decode Ways
practice.description: A message of letters `'A'`–`'Z'` is encoded as `'1'`–`'26'`. Given a string `s` containing only digits, return the number of ways to decode it.

editorial.summary: Use linear DP where `dp[i]` adds `dp[i - 1]` if `s[i - 1] != '0'` and adds `dp[i - 2]` if `10 <= int(s[i - 2:i]) <= 26`.
hints: A leading `'0'` cannot be decoded at all.
Two-digit codes must be between `10` and `26` inclusive.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: `'0'` alone is invalid; `'06'` is also invalid as a 2-digit code. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n) time and O(1) space limits.
approachSteps: For `i` from `1` to `len(s) - 1`, compute `curr` from 1-digit and 2-digit transitions, then shift.
pitfalls: `'0'` alone is invalid; `'06'` is also invalid as a 2-digit code.

practice.title: Coin Change II
practice.description:
A kiosk supports several token denominations. The operator wants to count the distinct ways to make change, ignoring the order of the tokens.

Given an integer array `coins` representing unique coin denominations and an integer `amount`, return the number of combinations (order does not matter) that make up `amount`.

editorial.summary: Iterate coins in the outer loop and amounts forward in the inner loop (`dp[a] += dp[a - c]`) to count unordered combinations without permutations.
hints: Outer loop over `coins` guarantees each combination is counted once in canonical coin order.
Base case `dp[0] = 1`.

Boundary edge cases & complexity: Putting `amount` in the outer loop counts ordered permutations instead of combinations. Verify your solution strictly meets O(amount * len(coins)) time and O(amount) space limits.
approachSteps: For each `c` in `coins`, for `a` from `c` to `amount`, add `dp[a - c]` to `dp[a]`.
pitfalls: Putting `amount` in the outer loop counts ordered permutations instead of combinations.

practice.title: Target Sum
practice.description: You are given an integer array `nums` of non-negative integers and an integer `target`. Assign either `'+'` or `'-'` before each integer in `nums` and return the number of different expressions that evaluate to `target`.

examples.explanation: Five ways to place one minus sign and four plus signs.

editorial.summary: Transform `P - N = target` and `P + N = total` into `P = (total + target) / 2`, then solve 0/1 subset-sum counting.
hints: If `abs(target) > total` or `(total + target)` is odd, return `0`.
Iterate sums backward from `pos` down to `x` so each item is used once.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Elements equal to `0` naturally double ways when iterating down to `x = 0`. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n * pos) time and O(pos) space limits.
approachSteps: Compute `total = sum(nums)`. Check `abs(target) <= total` and `(total + target) % 2 == 0`.
For each `x` in `nums`, loop `s` from `pos` down to `x`: `dp[s] += dp[s - x]`.
pitfalls: Elements equal to `0` naturally double ways when iterating down to `x = 0`.

practice.title: Triangle
practice.description: Given a `triangle` array, return the minimum path sum from top to bottom where at each step you may move to index `i` or `i + 1` on the row below.

editorial.summary: Collapse the triangle bottom-up starting from the last row: `dp[i] = row[i] + min(dp[i], dp[i + 1])`.
hints: Bottom-up eliminates boundary checks at row edges.
After reaching row 0, `dp[0]` holds the global minimum path sum.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Make a copy of the last row so you don't mutate the caller's input. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n^2) time and O(n) space limits.
approachSteps: Iterate rows from `len - 2` down to `0`, updating `dp[i] = triangle[r][i] + min(dp[i], dp[i + 1])`.
pitfalls: Make a copy of the last row so you don't mutate the caller's input.

practice.title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
practice.description: Given a string `s`, find the length of the longest palindromic subsequence in `s`.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.

editorial.summary: The longest palindromic subsequence of `s` is identical to the Longest Common Subsequence of `s` and `reversed(s)` (or solved via interval DP).
hints: Subsequence characters do not have to be contiguous.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Do not confuse subsequence with contiguous substring. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n^2) time and O(n) space limits.
approachSteps: Compute LCS of `s` and `t` using a 1D rolling row.
pitfalls: Do not confuse subsequence with contiguous substring.

practice.title: Interleaving String
practice.description: Given strings `s1`, `s2`, and `s3`, return `true` if `s3` is formed by an interleaving of `s1` and `s2` (preserving the relative order of characters from both `s1` and `s2`).

editorial.summary: Let `dp[i][j]` be whether `s1[:i]` and `s2[:j]` interleave to form `s3[:i + j]`, compressed to a 1D boolean array.
hints: First check `len(s1) + len(s2) == len(s3)`.
`dp[j]` updates from top (`dp[j] and s1[i-1] == s3[i+j-1]`) or left (`dp[j-1] and s2[j-1] == s3[i+j-1]`).
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Never skip the initial length check `len(s1) + len(s2) == len(s3)`. Verify your solution strictly meets O(m * n) time and O(n) space limits.
pitfalls: Never skip the initial length check `len(s1) + len(s2) == len(s3)`.

practice.title: Regular Expression Matching
practice.description: Given an input string `s` and a pattern `p`, implement regular expression matching with support for `'.'` (matches any single character) and `'*'` (matches zero or more of the preceding element). The matching must cover the entire input string.
constraints: Every '*' is preceded by a valid character.

editorial.summary: Use 2D DP (or memoized recursion) on `(i, j)`: when `p[j + 1] == '*'`, either skip the `x*` pair (`j + 2`) or consume one matching char in `s` (`i + 1, j`).

practice.title: Permutations
practice.description: Given an array `nums` of distinct integers, return all possible permutations in any order.
constraints: All integers of nums are unique.

editorial.summary: Swap each candidate into position `start`, recurse on `start + 1`, and swap back to restore state.
hints: In-place swapping avoids allocating a `used` array.
Record a copy `nums[:]` when `start == len(nums)`.
Boundary edge cases & complexity: Always append a shallow copy `nums[:]`. Verify your solution strictly meets O(n * n!) time and O(n) stack space limits.
approachSteps: For `i` in `range(start, n)`, swap `nums[start]` and `nums[i]`, recurse `bt(start + 1)`, swap back.
pitfalls: Always append a shallow copy `nums[:]`.

referenceCode.code:
def permute(nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
    res = []
    arr = list(nums)
    n = len(arr)
    def bt(start):
        if start == n:
            res.append(arr[:])
            return
        for i in range(start, n):
            arr[start], arr[i] = arr[i], arr[start]
            bt(start + 1)
            arr[start], arr[i] = arr[i], arr[start]
    bt(0)
    return res

Algorithmic Mechanics: Compare `abs(nums[l])` and `abs(nums[r])`. Fill `res[pos]` from `n - 1` down to `0` picking the larger square from ends.

referenceCode.code:
def sorted_squares(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums); res = [0] * n
    l, r = 0, n - 1
    for p in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        if abs(nums[l]) > abs(nums[r]): res[p] = nums[l] * nums[l]; l += 1
        else: res[p] = nums[r] * nums[r]; r -= 1
    return res

referenceCode.code:
def three_sum_closest(nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    a = sorted(nums); n = len(a); best = a[0] + a[1] + a[2]
    for i in range(n - 2):
        l, r = i + 1, n - 1
        while l < r:
            s = a[i] + a[l] + a[r]
            if abs(s - target) < abs(best - target): best = s
            if s == target: return target
            if s < target: l += 1
            else: r -= 1
    return best

from collections import deque

    class Node:
        def __init__(self, v): self.val, self.left, self.right = v, None, None
    head = Node(root[0])
    q = deque([head])
    i = 1
    while q and i < len(root):
        cur = q.popleft()
        if i < len(root) and root[i] is not None:
            cur.left = Node(root[i])
            q.append(cur.left)
        i += 1
        if i < len(root) and root[i] is not None:
            cur.right = Node(root[i])
            q.append(cur.right)
        i += 1
    stack = []
    cur = head
    prev = None
    best = float('inf')
    while stack or cur:
        while cur:
            stack.append(cur)
            cur = cur.left
        cur = stack.pop()
        if prev is not None:
            best = min(best, cur.val - prev)
        prev = cur.val
        cur = cur.right
    return best

    lps = [0] * m; ln = 0; i = 1

def wire_roundtrip(packets: list[str]) -> list[str]:

        i = j + 1 + L
    return out
